questions.question: What are the three pillars of IAM and which AWS service handles each?
questions.answer: Authentication (who is making the call) — handled by credential types (passwords, access keys, STS tokens, federated assertions). Authorization (is the caller permitted) — handled by IAM policy evaluation. Audibility (who did what, when, from where) — handled by AWS CloudTrail.

questions.question: What is the difference between an IAM user, an IAM group, and an IAM role?
questions.answer: IAM user: long-lived identity for a human or legacy workload, with username/password and optional access keys. IAM group: a permission management container — NOT an identity. Holds users and policies; cannot make API calls. IAM role: a temporary identity assumed via AWS STS; issues short-lived credentials; used for workloads and cross-account access.

questions.question: What is the IAM three-step evaluation rule?
questions.answer: Step 1: Is there an explicit Deny anywhere in the evaluated policies? If yes, deny — evaluation stops. Step 2: Is there an explicit Allow? If yes, allow. Step 3: If neither applies, implicit deny by default. The rule is invariant across all policy types and account boundaries.

questions.question: Why must the root user be locked away after initial AWS account setup?
questions.answer: The root user is unconstrained by any IAM policy, SCP, or permission boundary — it has 100% blast radius. A compromised root credential is the worst possible AWS security incident with no recovery path other than full account closure. The root user should only be used for ~5 tasks (closing account, changing root email/password, restoring IAM access, billing setup). For daily work, use an IAM user or IAM Identity Center federated identity.

questions.question: What is the least-privilege principle and how do you grade a policy against it?
questions.answer: Least privilege means granting the smallest action scope and resource scope that satisfies the functional requirement. Grade policies on two independent axes: Action scope (Narrow = specific API like s3:GetObject; Medium = service wildcard like s3:Get*; Wide = s3:*). Resource scope (Narrow = specific ARN with prefix; Medium = one bucket; Wide = *). A well-formed policy is narrow on both axes. Wide on either axis is almost never the right answer.

questions.question: What is the difference between identity-based and resource-based policies?
questions.answer: Identity-based: attached to IAM principals (users, groups, roles). Answers 'what can this principal do?' Principal element is implicit. Cannot grant cross-account access by itself. Resource-based: attached to AWS resources (S3, KMS, SQS, SNS, Lambda, ECR, EFS, API Gateway, Secrets Manager). Answers 'who can do what to this resource?' Requires explicit Principal element. Can grant cross-account access. Can enforce absolute denies.

questions.question: What is the difference between aws:MultiFactorAuthPresent and aws:MultiFactorAuthAge?
questions.answer: MultiFactorAuthPresent: boolean, set to true at session start if MFA was used, remains true for the entire session lifetime. Does NOT protect against session hijacking. MultiFactorAuthAge: numeric seconds since MFA credential was issued, increases as session ages. Use with NumericLessThan (e.g., 900) to require fresh MFA. Defends against session hijacking. Use Present for read-only operations; use Age for destructive operations.

questions.question: Why is the S3 ARN format unique compared to other AWS services?
questions.answer: S3 ARN omits both the region and account ID. Format: arn:aws:s3:::bucket-name/prefix/* — no region, no account-id. All other services include region and account ID. This is because S3 bucket names are globally unique — the bucket name itself is sufficient to identify the resource globally. This is the most commonly tested ARN format on the SAA-C03 exam.

questions.question: Which 9 AWS services support resource-based policies?
questions.answer: S3, KMS, SQS, SNS, Lambda, ECR, EFS, API Gateway, and Secrets Manager. All other AWS services rely on identity-based policies only. Remember: these are the services where you can attach a policy directly to the resource rather than to the IAM identity.

questions.question: Can IAM groups be principals in a resource-based policy like an S3 bucket policy?
questions.answer: No. IAM groups are containers for permission management, not identities. When writing a bucket policy, you must reference the underlying IAM users or roles — not the groups they belong to. Groups cannot make API calls; only the users inside the group can. This is a common exam trap.

questions.question: Describe a scenario where you would use IAM groups vs IAM roles to manage permissions.
questions.answer: (Situation) A team of 40 engineers needed the same baseline S3 read permissions. Each had policies attached directly. (Task) Simplify permission management and reduce policy attachment count by 80%. (Action) Created a DataEngineers group, attached the S3 read policy once to the group, removed individual policies, added all 40 users to the group. (Result) Future permission changes are one-line edits at the group level. New engineers get permissions just by being added to the group.

questions.question: Walk me through how you would debug an Access Denied error for an IAM role that has an explicit Allow for s3:GetObject.
questions.answer: (Situation) Developer role has Allow for s3:GetObject but API returns Access Denied. (Task) Find the source of the denial. (Action) Applied the three-step rule. Step 1: looked for explicit denies in: (1) SCP in the account's organization, (2) permission boundary on the role, (3) S3 bucket policy, (4) session policy if the role was assumed with session policies. Found an SCP that denied s3:GetObject on production buckets for all developer roles. (Result) The Allow was overridden by the SCP explicit Deny — removed the SCP restriction for the specific deployment role.

questions.question: How would you implement cross-account access from an EC2 workload in Account B to a KMS-encrypted S3 bucket in Account A without using long-lived credentials?
questions.answer: (Situation) Analytics EC2 in Account B needs read access to encrypted videos in Account A. No long-lived credentials allowed. (Task) Implement secure cross-account access. (Action) Created DataAnalystRole in Account A with trust policy allowing Account B to assume it. Role policy allows s3:GetObject on the bucket and kms:Decrypt on the key. Updated KMS key policy to also allow kms:Decrypt for the role (two-pronged requirement). Created instance profile in Account B with sts:AssumeRole permission. Attached profile to EC2 instances. Enabled CloudTrail data events on the S3 bucket. (Result) Instances assume the role via STS, receive temporary credentials, read videos, credentials expire automatically. Zero access keys on instances.

questions.question: A security team needs to ensure data analysts can never delete production S3 data, regardless of any future IAM policy changes. What mechanism do you use and why?
questions.answer: (Situation) Risk of accidental or malicious deletion of production data by analysts. (Task) Enforce no-deletion absolutely. (Action) Added a resource-based bucket policy with an explicit Deny on s3:DeleteObject and s3:DeleteObjectVersion for the DataAnalystRole principal. This is a resource-based explicit deny, which overrides any Allow in any policy type. (Result) Even if someone in the future accidentally attaches a policy granting delete permissions to the analyst role, the bucket policy explicit deny wins — the deletion is impossible. Identity-based allows cannot override resource-based explicit denies.

questions.question: How would you enforce that deletion of production resources requires a fresh MFA challenge within the last 15 minutes, even if the user already authenticated with MFA at sign-in this morning?
questions.answer: (Situation) Users sign in once with MFA. After 8 hours, their session is still MFA-authenticated (MultiFactorAuthPresent = true) but could be hijacked. (Task) Require fresh MFA on destructive actions. (Action) Added IAM policy condition NumericLessThan: aws:MultiFactorAuthAge: 900 to the policies granting deletion permissions. MultiFactorAuthPresent alone is insufficient because it stays true for the session lifetime. (Result) Deletion attempts more than 15 minutes after last MFA challenge are denied. User must re-authenticate with MFA before deleting production resources, defending against session hijacking.

questions.question: A developer argues that using s3:* with a narrow resource ARN (specific bucket) is acceptable because the resource scope limits the blast radius. How do you respond?
questions.answer: (Situation) Developer policy uses s3:* on arn:aws:s3:::acme-reports/*. (Task) Evaluate the security risk. (Action) Explained that s3:* includes PutBucketPolicy, DeleteBucket, PutBucketAcl, PutBucketCors — admin-level actions the application never needs. A narrow resource with wide action scope still violates least privilege. Used the two-axis grading rubric: narrow resource = good, wide action = fail. (Result) Tightened to exactly the APIs the application uses (s3:GetObject, s3:PutObject). Zero functional impact, significant reduction in blast radius.

questions.question: What is the source account and destination account in a cross-account access scenario, and why does it matter?
questions.answer: (Situation) EC2 in Account B accesses S3 in Account A via role assumption. (Task) Correctly identify source and destination for debugging. (Action) Explained: the source account is the one making the call (Account B — where the request originates). The destination account is the one holding the resource (Account A — where S3 and the role exist). This matters for debugging because when a cross-account call fails: (1) principal's IAM policy check is in the source account, (2) role trust policy, bucket policy, and KMS key policy checks are all in the destination account. (Result) Correctly identifying source vs destination cuts debugging time in half.

questions.question: How do permission boundaries differ from SCPs, and when would you use each?
questions.answer: (Situation) Need to limit how much permission a developer can grant themselves, AND limit what all accounts in an OU can do. (Task) Choose the right mechanism. (Action) Used permission boundaries on developer IAM users to cap their maximum effective permissions to developer-scope only — even if they write a policy that says Allow: *, the boundary intersection prevents escalation. Used SCPs at the AWS Organizations level to deny certain actions (like creating IAM admin users) across all member accounts. (Result) Permission boundaries control per-identity blast radius. SCPs control per-account or per-OU blast radius.

questions.question: Explain the ACME Media cross-account architecture: what role does STS play, and what happens after the role is assumed?
questions.answer: (Situation) EC2 in Account B needs KMS-encrypted S3 data from Account A without long-lived credentials. (Task) Explain the full flow including STS. (Action) Instance profile on EC2 has sts:AssumeRole permission for Account A's DataAnalystRole. EC2 calls STS AssumeRole. STS checks: (a) the role's trust policy allows Account B, (b) the caller has AssumeRole permission. STS issues temporary credentials (access key, secret, session token) valid for typically 1 hour. EC2 uses these to call s3:GetObject and kms:Decrypt. IAM evaluates as a same-account call from the assumed role identity. Once credentials expire, access is automatically revoked. (Result) Zero long-lived credentials on instances. Every access is time-bounded and audited.

questions.question: What are the four places to check when a cross-account call to a KMS-encrypted S3 bucket fails with Access Denied?
questions.answer: (Situation) Cross-account S3 access denied despite believing permissions are correct. (Task) Debug systematically. (Action) In order: (1) Principal's IAM policy in the SOURCE account — does the EC2 instance profile allow sts:AssumeRole on the role ARN? (2) Role trust policy in the DESTINATION account — does the trust policy allow the source account to assume the role? (3) Bucket policy in the DESTINATION account — is there an explicit deny blocking the role? (4) KMS key policy in the DESTINATION account — does the key policy allow kms:Decrypt for the role? (Result) All four must be correct simultaneously. Missing even one causes Access Denied.

questions.question: Design an IAM architecture for a company that has 200 engineers in 4 departments, uses multiple AWS accounts, needs SSO from their corporate Active Directory, and must enforce MFA on all high-privilege actions.
questions.answer: Use AWS IAM Identity Center as the central identity hub — federated to the corporate Active Directory via SAML. Create permission sets in Identity Center that map to job functions (DataEngineer, DevOps, SecurityAudit, ReadOnly). Assign permission sets to AWS accounts in the organization via IAM Identity Center account assignments. Use AWS Organizations + SCPs to enforce guardrails at the OU level (e.g., deny non-us-east-1 regions for compliance). Add condition keys (MultiFactorAuthAge: 900) to permission sets for any destructive actions. Use CloudTrail organization trail to capture all events across all accounts. Use AWS Access Analyzer to continuously audit permissions. Result: single pane of glass identity management, no per-account IAM users to manage, full audit trail, automatic deprovisioning when an employee leaves the IdP.

questions.question: A company's IAM architecture audit reveals 300 policies directly attached to 300 individual IAM users. Propose a migration plan to a group-based model and describe the risk controls.
questions.answer: Phase 1 (Analysis): Use IAM Access Analyzer and AWS Config to map current permissions per user. Identify permission clusters — groups of users with near-identical permission sets. Phase 2 (Group Design): Create IAM groups aligned to job functions, not environment. Avoid environment-per-group anti-pattern. Phase 3 (Policy Consolidation): For each group, write one consolidated policy at the group level using the union of what users in that cluster actually need. Grade each new policy on the two-axis rubric. Phase 4 (Migration): In a test account, attach users to new groups, validate access. Use IAM policy simulator. In production, use a cut-over window. Phase 5 (Cleanup): After 2 weeks validation, remove direct user policy attachments. Risk controls: keep old policies in a disabled state for rollback. Result: ~80% reduction in policy attachment count, one-line changes for future permission updates.

questions.question: Explain how you would architect a multi-region, multi-account AWS organization with guardrails that prevent any account from disabling CloudTrail.
questions.answer: Use AWS Organizations with a management account at the root. Create an OU structure (Security OU, Workload OU, Sandbox OU). Apply an SCP at the root that explicitly denies cloudtrail:StopLogging and cloudtrail:DeleteTrail for all principals except the security automation role. Create an organization-level CloudTrail trail in the Security OU management account — this captures events across all member accounts and cannot be disabled by member account admins. Use AWS Config organization conformance packs to detect and auto-remediate any drift. Use IAM Identity Center for unified access. Result: even an account admin with AdministratorAccess cannot disable CloudTrail because the SCP explicit deny overrides any allow.

questions.question: A security engineer discovers that a production Lambda function has been given s3:* on *. What is the immediate risk and how do you remediate without breaking the function?
questions.answer: Immediate risk: the Lambda function can read, write, delete, and reconfigure any S3 bucket in the account — including modifying bucket policies and ACLs. If the function is exploited (code injection, SSRF), the attacker has full S3 control. Remediation: (1) Use IAM Access Analyzer to identify which S3 actions the Lambda has actually called in the past 90 days. (2) Draft a narrow policy: only the specific APIs observed (e.g., s3:GetObject, s3:PutObject) on the specific bucket ARN the function uses. (3) Test in a staging environment. (4) Deploy the narrow policy, verify function works. (5) Remove the wildcard policy. Risk control: use a permission boundary on the Lambda's execution role to cap maximum permissions. Never deploy with s3:* in production.

questions.question: Explain the concept of 'defense in depth' in IAM and show how the ACME Media architecture implements it with at least three distinct layers.
questions.answer: Defense in depth means that even if one security control fails, multiple independent controls remain. ACME Media implements it as: Layer 1 (Identity control) — DataAnalystRole has an identity-based policy with only s3:GetObject and kms:Decrypt with MultiFactorAuthAge: 900. Even if an attacker has the role's temporary credentials, they cannot delete data and must have authenticated with MFA within 15 minutes. Layer 2 (Resource control) — S3 bucket policy has an explicit Deny on DeleteObject for DataAnalystRole. Even if the role policy were changed to include Delete, the bucket policy explicit deny overrides it. Layer 3 (Permission boundary on developers) — Developers who temporarily assume DataAnalystRole cannot escalate their effective permissions beyond the intersection of their boundary and the role. Layer 4 (Audit) — CloudTrail data events capture every API call. Even if layers 1-3 were somehow bypassed, the audit trail provides detection and forensics. Result: no single misconfiguration can compromise data integrity.
